A passage titled “Mathematics within Christian philosophy” describes how Greek philosophical manuscripts became less accessible in Western Europe after the fall of the Roman Empire, as Greek literacy declined and manuscripts were preserved in small monasteries. It contrasts early Christian distance from pagan Greek philosophers with later Christian arguments that mathematics suited belief in a God who favored rules and laws.

Saint Augustine (354–430) was an autodidact and later a Church Father. Although Augustine did not write specifically about geometry or arithmetic, in *De Libero Arbitrio* (*On Free Choice of the Will*), written between 387 and 395, he compared arithmetic knowledge to divine revelation. He argued that numerical truths are certain and unchanging, cannot be established through bodily senses across innumerable numbers, and are perceived through an inner light and shared by reasoning people.

The passage says later Christian thinkers interpreted Augustine’s account of mathematical truth as sanctifying mathematical knowledge. It also notes the prominence of numbers and numerology in Old Testament books and the belief, held by some Christian thinkers into the 11th century, that God must have known geometry because Creation appeared harmonious, with perfect spheres and circular orbits.

Boethius (480–524/525), from a wealthy and politically influential family, knew Greek philosophers and was known for translating works by Aristotle and Plato. Unlike Augustine, Boethius consciously emphasized Pythagorean number theory and arithmetic over geometry. His *De institutione arithmetica* presented medieval arithmetic, emphasized numerological interpretation, and served as an introduction to music theory.

Boethius provided rules for computus, the calculation of time used in establishing a Biblical calendar and calculating Easter. The Council of Nicaea in 325 established Easter as the first Sunday after the first full moon in spring. The passage says *De institutione arithmetica* was valuable as a practical calculation guide, although the arithmetic and astronomy needed for the calculations are not included in the surviving text described there.

The passage describes a Roman-law inheritance case in the *Pandectae*: a man stipulated that his pregnant wife receive one-third of the inheritance if she bore a son, or two-thirds if she bore a daughter, with the remainder going to the child. After his death, the wife bore twins of different sexes. Although the passage says the problem is not decidable by present-day ideas, a ratio-based verdict was proposed as a fair solution.

During the Carolingian Renaissance around 800 AD, education for the land-owning aristocracy was organized around the Artes liberales, divided into the trivium and quadrivium. The trivium comprised grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic; the quadrivium comprised arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy.

A caption in the supplied passage identifies an illustration as a page from a tenth-century Boethius manuscript at Lund University Library. In its upper-right corner, powers of three are shown in Roman numerals: I, III, VIIII, XXVII, LXXXI, and CCXLIII; the caption notes the numerological appeal of powers of three from a Christian perspective.
